nameStory: This fungus earned its "jellied false coral" name because it looks remarkably like underwater coral but has a distinctive jelly-like, gelatinous texture when fresh. The "false" part distinguishes it from true coral fungi, which are firmer and belong to completely different fungal families. Early mycologist Lewis David von Schweinitz first described this species, which is why it carries his name scientifically.
description: The jellied false coral fungus is a fascinating gelatinous fungus that forms translucent, coral-like branches rising from decaying wood. When fresh, it has a clear to whitish, jelly-like appearance that can look almost glass-like in the right light. The branching structure typically reaches 1-3 inches tall and wide, with multiple finger-like projections that fork and divide. During dry periods, it shrinks down to a hard, dark crust, but swells back up after rain like a natural sponge.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Distinctly gelatinous and jelly-like when moist, feeling rubbery yet delicate to the touch - like firm Jell-O that might tear if handled roughly

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Forms coral-like branches that fork and divide, creating an intricate branching pattern without any cap or stem structure

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent white to clear when fresh and moist, becoming dark brown to black when dried out, with a glass-like transparency in good light

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows directly from decaying hardwood logs and branches, never found on the ground or on living trees

idTips.label: Weather Response
idTips.description: Dramatically shrinks to a hard, dark crust during dry weather but quickly swells back to full size after rain - this transformation is diagnostic

habitat: Look for jellied false coral on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England. It particularly favors oak, maple, and beech wood that's been decomposing for at least a year or two. You'll often find it in moist, shaded areas where the wood stays damp longer, from low-elevation forests up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Begins appearing in late spring as temperatures warm and moisture increases, often looking fresh and translucent after spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Most visible during humid summer months, especially after thunderstorms when the gelatinous fruiting bodies swell to full size and become nearly transparent.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting through fall, particularly abundant during wet autumn weather, though may start showing more brownish coloration.
seasonality.winter: Typically shrunk down to dark, crusty patches during winter dry spells, but can rehydrate during winter thaws and mild, wet periods.

funFact: This fungus can lose up to 90% of its water content and appear completely dead as a black crust, then within hours of rainfall, it absorbs water and springs back to life like a botanical resurrection - some specimens have been observed doing this revival act for several years running!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with white coral jelly fungus, but jellied false coral is more translucent and delicate, while white coral jelly fungus is more opaque white and has a firmer, less transparent appearance. Remember: if it looks like clear jelly coral, it's probably jellied false coral; if it's more solid white coral, it's likely the white coral jelly fungus.
contextualKnowledge: The "false coral" name can be confusing since there are many coral-shaped fungi - this one specifically refers to the jelly-like texture that distinguishes it from the firmer "true" coral fungi in other families. Despite looking fragile, these gelatinous fungi are actually quite resilient and can survive repeated drying and rehydrating cycles.
compareHints: Unlike its relative white coral jelly fungus which maintains a more consistently white, opaque appearance, jellied false coral is notably more translucent and glass-like. The enveloping crust (Sebacina incrustans) forms flat, crust-like patches rather than the distinctive branching coral structure. Among the Sebacina genus, jellied false coral is unique for its combination of coral-like branching and high translucency when fresh.
